passage: Rain taps on the kitchen window of a small flat in Leeds. Kwame, two, tugs his mother's sleeve and points at the tap. "Wa-wa," he says. Zeynep fills his cup. When he reaches for the hot oven door, she says, "No, hot," and he pulls his hand back, watching her face. Later the old cat curls on the rug. Kwame kneels, strokes her back with one flat palm, slow, and whispers, "Soft kitty."

qa.q: What did Kwame say when he wanted a drink?
qa.a: He points at the tap and says "Wa-wa."

qa.q: What does Kwame watching his mother's face suggest about how he took her warning?
qa.a: He pulled his hand back and watched her face, which suggests he was checking her and taking the "No, hot" seriously.

qa.q: How could Zeynep keep encouraging Kwame's gentle touch with the cat?
qa.a: She could notice it out loud, like "Gentle hands, the cat likes that," so he links his soft stroking with the cat staying calm. 🙂

qa.q: What might the cat experience because of Kwame's slow stroking?
qa.a: The old cat can stay relaxed on the rug instead of moving away, because his touch is calm rather than grabbing.

grounding: It shows a toddler asking for a need, heeding a parent's limit and touching an animal gently.

passage: My little brother Ramesh is two. This morning I watched him while Amma bathed. He came to me holding his bottom and said, "Didi, potty!" I took him quickly. Then he went for Amma's steel tiffin on the shelf. I said, "That's Amma's, no." He stopped, looked at me for a long time, and put his hands behind his back. When our neighbour's puppy came in, he patted its head very lightly, like it might break. — Bhavna

qa.q: Who looked after Ramesh while Amma bathed?
qa.a: His sister Bhavna watched him.

qa.q: What might Ramesh have been thinking when he put his hands behind his back?
qa.a: He may have wanted the tiffin but was trying to follow the rule; Bhavna can only guess, since she saw the long look, not his thoughts.

qa.q: How could Bhavna or Amma help Ramesh keep telling them what he needs?
qa.a: They can respond quickly and calmly when he says things like "potty," so he learns that speaking up works.

qa.q: How does Bhavna seem to see her brother's gentleness with the puppy?
qa.a: She seems a little amused and proud, describing his pat as so light it was like the puppy might break.

grounding: An older sister observes a toddler naming a toilet need, stopping at a family limit, and patting a puppy gently.

passage:
Monday: Nandini, almost two, grabbed Bruno's ear and yanked. The dog yelped. Gautam knelt, took her hand and moved it slowly down Bruno's back. "Soft, like this."
Thursday: She reached for Bruno again, stopped, and patted twice, looking up at Papa. When Gautam said, "Papa is on the phone, wait," she sat down with her doll.
The next Monday: "Papa, milk," she said, carrying her cup. Then she stroked Bruno and whispered, "Soft."

qa.q: What did Nandini do to Bruno on Monday?
qa.a: She grabbed Bruno's ear and yanked, and the dog yelped.

qa.q: Why do you think Nandini looked up at Papa after patting Bruno on Thursday?
qa.a: She probably wanted to check that she was doing it right and hoped Papa noticed her soft touch.

qa.q: What worked well in how Gautam taught gentle touch?
qa.a: He showed her with her own hand instead of scolding, and gave simple words, "Soft, like this," that she later repeated herself.

qa.q: How is life different for Bruno by the next Monday?
qa.a: Bruno is stroked instead of yanked, so being near Nandini is probably calmer and safer for him.

grounding: Over several days a toddler learns gentle touch with a dog, waits for her father, and asks for milk in words.

passage: Teacher's note, Tuesday. Elizabeth and a friend sat on opposite sides of the toy farm. Elizabeth said, "Look at the red door!" Her friend frowned: "There's no door." Elizabeth stood, walked round the table and crouched. "Oh! From here it's just a wall." She came back and turned the barn halfway so both could see the door. I asked what she noticed. "She sees the back side, I see the front." 😊 Next, I'll try a picture-drawing game from two sides. — Ms Manjula

qa.q: What did Elizabeth do after her friend said there was no door?
qa.a: She walked round the table, crouched, and saw that from there it was just a wall.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth's "Oh!" suggest about what she realised?
qa.a: It suggests surprise as she understood that her friend's side of the barn really looked different from her own.

qa.q: How could Ms Manjula build on this moment?
qa.a: Her planned game of drawing the same object from two sides lets Elizabeth keep checking what others can see.

qa.q: How might the friend feel once Elizabeth turned the barn?
qa.a: She would likely feel understood rather than wrong, since now she could see the door too. 🙂

grounding: A teacher records a child discovering that her friend sees a different side of the same toy barn.

passage: Behind the cowshed in their village, Payal squatted beside the buffalo and pointed. "Saurabh Bhaiya, the calf is drinking!" From the other side, her brother called, "Which calf?" Payal giggled, then paused. The big buffalo was between them. She ran around the tail and pulled him by the hand. "You can't see it from there. The buffalo is blocking you." Saurabh grinned as the tiny calf nudged its mother's belly. "Now I see it."

qa.q: What was between Payal and her brother?
qa.a: The big buffalo was between them.

qa.q: Why do you think Payal paused after giggling?
qa.a: She seems to have realised that her brother's view was blocked, so his question was not silly after all.

qa.q: What was good about the way Payal solved the problem?
qa.a: Instead of repeating herself, she brought him to her side so he could see the calf for himself.

qa.q: What would change if the calf had been on Saurabh's side instead?
qa.a: Then he would see it and Payal might be the one asking "Which calf?", showing that each view depends on where you stand.

grounding: A village girl figures out that her brother cannot see the calf because the buffalo blocks his view.

passage: Saturday morning in a Madrid flat, Alejandro held up his picture book to Nadia, who sat facing him on the sofa. "See the dragon?" Nadia shook her head. "I only see the cover, Ale." Alejandro looked at the page, then at her. Slowly he turned the book around. "Now?" "Now I see a green dragon," she said. He tried it again with the next page, flipping it toward her each time before he read.

qa.q: Where were Alejandro and Nadia sitting?
qa.a: They sat facing each other on the sofa in a Madrid flat.

qa.q: What was Alejandro thinking when he looked at the page and then at Nadia?
qa.a: He seemed to be working out that the picture was facing only him, so Nadia could not see what he saw.

qa.q: How could Nadia help Alejandro practise this more?
qa.a: She could keep asking, "What can I see from here?" so he checks her side before showing things.

qa.q: What is it like for Nadia once Alejandro starts flipping each page toward her?
qa.a: She can finally join in the story instead of staring at a cover, which makes reading together fun for her.

grounding: A boy learns his sister sees only the cover of a book held facing him, and turns it so she can see.

passage:
"Maria Didi, where are you putting Nani's glasses?"
"On the shelf, Akash. They'll get broken on the chair."
"But Nani went to the market. She saw them on the chair."
"Yes. So when she comes back, where will she look?"
"On the chair!" Akash laughed. "But they're not there!"
"Why will she look there?"
"Because she didn't see you move them. She thinks they're still on the chair."
"Good thinking. Let's tell her when she's home."

qa.q: Where did Maria put Nani's glasses?
qa.a: She put them on the shelf so they would not get broken on the chair.

qa.q: Why does Akash think Nani will look on the chair?
qa.a: He knows Nani didn't see Maria move them, so she still believes they are on the chair even though that is wrong.

qa.q: What did Maria do that helped Akash understand?
qa.a: She asked questions like "Where will she look?" and let him explain the reason himself.

qa.q: How might Nani feel if nobody told her about the move?
qa.a: She might be puzzled and worried when she finds the chair empty, so telling her saves her a scare.

grounding: A boy works out that his grandmother still believes her glasses are where she left them.

passage: Observation note, Class KG-B. During puppet time I put a ball in the blue box while Bunny puppet watched, then sent Bunny away. Teddy moved the ball to the red box. I asked, "Where will Bunny look?" Hafsa jumped up: "Blue box! Bunny didn't see Teddy." Two classmates said red. Hafsa explained, "But Bunny wasn't here!" 👏 Tomorrow I'll let Hafsa run the puppets so others can guess and explain their answers. — Saurabh Sir

qa.q: Which box did Teddy move the ball to?
qa.a: Teddy moved the ball to the red box.

qa.q: How can you tell Hafsa felt sure of her answer?
qa.a: She jumped up to answer and kept explaining, "But Bunny wasn't here!" even when two classmates said red.

qa.q: How could the teacher support the classmates who said red?
qa.a: Letting Hafsa run the puppets and asking children to explain their guesses gives them another turn to notice who saw what.

qa.q: How might the two classmates see Hafsa's answer at first?
qa.a: They might think she is wrong, because they know the ball is in the red box and have not yet thought about what Bunny saw.

grounding: A teacher notes a child predicting that a puppet will act on an out-of-date belief.

passage: In the afternoon heat, Reena's goat wandered from the shed to the shade by the well. Reena watched her lie down. Soon Harish Bhaiya came up the lane with his school bag. "I'll give Chhoti her water in the shed," he said, picking up the bucket. Reena covered her mouth and giggled. "Bhaiya thinks she's in the shed!" she told Amma. "He didn't see her go." Then she ran after him. "Bhaiya, she's by the well!"

qa.q: Where did the goat go to lie down?
qa.a: She wandered from the shed to the shade by the well.

qa.q: Why did Reena giggle when Harish picked up the bucket?
qa.a: She found it funny that he believed the goat was in the shed when she knew it wasn't.

qa.q: What choice did Reena make that was kind?
qa.a: After enjoying the joke, she ran after him to tell him the truth so he would not carry the bucket to an empty shed.

qa.q: How might Harish feel when he hears where Chhoti is?
qa.a: He would probably be relieved to save a trip and maybe amused that his little sister knew more than him this time.

grounding: A small-town girl realises her brother holds a mistaken belief about where the goat is.

passage: In Aaji's house in the kasba, Hrithik squeezed behind the rice sacks in the storeroom. "Ready!" he called. Aaji Usha shuffled in, peering. "Is Hrithik under the cot? No. In the steel cupboard? No." Hrithik pressed both hands over his mouth, shoulders shaking. She walked right past the sacks. She doesn't know, he thought, eyes shining. When she turned away, he jumped out. "Boo! You didn't find me!" Aaji clutched her chest and laughed.

qa.q: Where did Hrithik hide?
qa.a: He squeezed behind the rice sacks in the storeroom.

qa.q: What does Hrithik pressing his hands over his mouth suggest?
qa.a: He was bursting with glee and trying hard not to give himself away, because he knew Aaji did not know where he was.

qa.q: How could Aaji keep this game fun and fair?
qa.a: She can keep pretending to search in several places and then let Hrithik take a turn as the seeker too.

qa.q: What might Aaji be enjoying in this game?
qa.a: She seems to enjoy playing along and hamming up her surprise, which makes her grandson's trick feel like a success. 😊

grounding: A small-town boy delights in hiding from his grandmother, knowing she cannot see where he is.

passage: On a Lisbon beach, Mateo hid a white pebble in one fist and put both hands behind his back. He shuffled them around. "Which hand, Beatriz?" His big sister tapped the left. He opened it, empty, and squealed. "You don't know! Only I know!" The next time, he pressed his lips tight and tried to keep a straight face, but his eyes kept sliding to his right hand. Beatriz smiled and chose right.

qa.q: What did Mateo hide in his fist?
qa.a: He hid a white pebble.

qa.q: Why was Mateo so thrilled when Beatriz picked the empty hand?
qa.a: He was delighted to realise that she didn't know something he knew, which made the trick feel powerful and fun.

qa.q: What could Mateo try next time to keep his secret better?
qa.a: He could practise keeping his eyes still, since his glances toward the right hand gave the pebble away. 🤔

qa.q: How does Beatriz seem to see the game?
qa.a: She seems amused and kind, playing along and reading his eyes, which shows she enjoys the game with him.

grounding: A young boy discovers that his sister cannot know which hand holds the pebble unless he shows her.

passage: At the preschool, Suraj Sir covered his eyes and counted. Keerthana tucked the class teddy inside the dress-up basket, then pressed a finger to her lips at her friends. "Shh! Don't tell." Suraj Sir looked under the mats and behind the curtain, muttering, "Where could Teddy be?" Keerthana bounced on her toes. "He doesn't know!" she whispered. When he finally opened the basket, she shrieked with laughter and begged, "Again! Now you close your eyes!"

qa.q: Where did Keerthana hide the class teddy?
qa.a: She tucked it inside the dress-up basket.

qa.q: How can you tell Keerthana felt delighted to know something the teacher didn't?
qa.a: She bounced on her toes, whispered "He doesn't know!" and shrieked with laughter when he found it.

qa.q: How could Suraj Sir extend this game for the class?
qa.a: He could let children take turns hiding the teddy and ask, "Who knows where it is, and who doesn't?"

qa.q: What would change if Suraj Sir had peeked while counting?
qa.a: The trick would be spoiled, and Keerthana would miss the fun of seeing that others don't know everything she knows.

grounding: A preschooler hides a teddy and relishes that her teacher does not know where it is.

passage: Kavitha from the second floor was in the colony sandpit again this evening. I was on the bench with my book. Three kids had their own things going: one digging a hole, one filling cups, Kavitha making a "cake" with leaves. She handed the boy her spade and took his cup, chatting about her cake the whole time. He talked about his hole. Nobody built anything together, but they looked happy. — Lalit, neighbour

qa.q: What was Kavitha making in the sandpit?
qa.a: She was making a "cake" with leaves.

qa.q: What seems to have been Kavitha's mood while swapping toys and chatting?
qa.a: She looked happy and interested; Lalit only saw her from the bench, so he can guess at her mood but not know it for sure.

qa.q: How could an adult nearby support this kind of play?
qa.a: Offer enough spades and cups to go round and let the children chat and swap freely without forcing one shared project.

qa.q: How might the boy digging the hole experience playing near Kavitha?
qa.a: He gets company and a spade to use while still doing his own digging, which feels friendly without pressure.

grounding: A neighbour notices children sharing toys and talking in a sandpit while each pursues a separate project.

passage:
Monday: At the play table, Afreen and Bidisha rolled playdough side by side. Neither spoke. Afreen kept the star cutter close to her chest.
Wednesday: Bidisha pointed. "Can I have the star?" Afreen passed it over. "I'm making biscuits," she said. "I'm making a snake," said Bidisha.
The next Monday: They chattered nonstop, swapping cutters back and forth, Afreen with her biscuits and Bidisha with a whole snake family, each admiring the other's.

qa.q: What was Afreen making on Wednesday?
qa.a: She said she was making biscuits.

qa.q: What does Afreen holding the star cutter close on Monday suggest?
qa.a: She may have felt protective of it and not yet ready to share with Bidisha.

qa.q: How could a teacher gently encourage this change?
qa.a: Place the girls near each other with a few shared tools, so asking and swapping happen naturally.

qa.q: How is the play different for Bidisha by the next Monday?
qa.a: She now has a chatty partner who swaps cutters with her, even though they are still making different things.

grounding: Over days two girls move from silent side-by-side play to sharing and talking while each keeps her own creation.

passage: The power went out just as the rain began, and Farida's small front room grew dim and crowded. Arohi and Farida lay on the floor near the window with one tin of crayons between them. Arohi drew a rainbow, Farida a house. "Pass the blue?" "Here. My sky needs it too." They swapped, chattering about their own pictures while the rain drummed. When Farida's cousin squeezed in, they pushed the tin toward him.

qa.q: How many tins of crayons did Arohi and Farida have?
qa.a: They had one tin of crayons between them.

qa.q: Why do you think the girls kept talking while they drew?
qa.a: They seemed to enjoy each other's company and wanted to share what they were making, even with different pictures.

qa.q: What helped the girls cope with the power cut?
qa.a: Moving close to the window for light and sharing the one tin let them keep playing happily.

qa.q: How might the cousin feel when they push the tin toward him?
qa.a: He would probably feel welcome to join, even without being part of a shared plan. 🙂

grounding: During a power cut, two girls share crayons and chat, each drawing her own picture.

passage: At a beach near Melbourne, Bao and Dalia dug a moat around their sandcastle. "The waves keep filling it with sand!" Dalia groaned. Bao thought. "You dig, I'll make a wall." Dalia scooped while Bao patted wet sand into a bank. When a small wave slid in, the water filled the moat but stopped at the wall. They grabbed each other's hands and jumped. "We did it!" Then they made the wall taller, together.

qa.q: What did Bao make while Dalia dug?
qa.a: Bao patted wet sand into a bank to make a wall.

qa.q: How do Bao and Dalia feel when the wave stops at the wall?
qa.a: They feel proud and joyful, shown by grabbing hands, jumping and shouting "We did it!"

qa.q: Which choice made their plan work?
qa.a: Splitting the jobs, one digging and one building the wall, let them protect the moat faster than either could alone.

qa.q: What would change if Dalia had kept digging alone?
qa.a: The waves would likely keep filling the moat, and she might give up frustrated without Bao's wall.

grounding: Two children divide tasks to build a sand wall that protects their shared moat.

passage: In the anganwadi, Zainab and Ganga wanted the wooden train track to reach all the way to the door. "Not enough straight pieces," Ganga said. Zainab found curved ones in the basket. "Put two curves, it goes the same way." Ganga held the track steady while Zainab clicked pieces in. When the didi called lunch, the track stopped one step short. They asked to leave it, and after lunch they finished it, cheering as the engine rolled through.

qa.q: Where did the girls want the train track to reach?
qa.a: They wanted it to reach all the way to the door.

qa.q: What might Ganga have been worried about when she said there were not enough pieces?
qa.a: She may have feared they could not finish the track and reach the door.

qa.q: What went well in how they handled lunch interrupting?
qa.a: They asked to leave the track standing and came back after lunch to finish it.

qa.q: How might the anganwadi didi see their project?
qa.a: She may be impressed that two small children kept a shared goal through a break and worked it out together. 😊

grounding: Two children at a centre work together to build a train track that reaches the door.

passage: My cousin Wasim is five. On Sunday I watched him and his friend from next door try to build a block tower as high as the window. Wasim held the bottom steady with both hands. His friend stood on a stool and placed blocks. "Slowly, slowly," Wasim said. When it wobbled, they stopped and agreed to use the big blocks first. It reached the window. They both yelled for me to look. — Pankaj

qa.q: How high did the boys want their block tower to be?
qa.a: They wanted it as high as the window.

qa.q: What does "Slowly, slowly" suggest Wasim was feeling?
qa.a: He was probably careful and a bit nervous that the tower would fall, though Pankaj can only guess from his words.

qa.q: What could an adult do to help such teamwork continue?
qa.a: Stay nearby, keep the stool safe, and praise how they agreed to change plans when the tower wobbled.

qa.q: Why do you think the boys wanted Pankaj to look?
qa.a: They wanted someone to see and share their success, showing how proud they were of what they made together.

grounding: An older cousin watches two boys cooperate and change their plan to build a tall block tower.

passage: The school van would honk in ten minutes, but Aadhya and Wasim were deep in a game of "house" under the dining table. "I'm the mummy and you're the baby," Aadhya said. Wasim shook his head. "I want to be the papa who cooks." Aadhya thought. "Okay, you cook, I go to office, and the teddy is the baby." They served a pretend dal. When the van honked, Wasim said, "Tomorrow the baby has a birthday."

qa.q: Where were Aadhya and Wasim playing?
qa.a: They were playing "house" under the dining table.

qa.q: Why did Wasim shake his head at Aadhya's first plan?
qa.a: He did not want to be the baby; he wanted a bigger part as the papa who cooks.

qa.q: What made their negotiation work?
qa.a: Aadhya listened and changed the plan so both had roles they liked, and the teddy became the baby.

qa.q: How might the teddy's role change the game for both children?
qa.a: It gives them someone to care for together, and it lets Wasim plan the next part of their story.

grounding: Two children negotiate roles and storyline in a game of house before the school van arrives.

passage: In the colony stairwell of their Pune building, Vasudha set out leaves and bottle caps on a step. "This is my shop. You come to buy," she told Sonali. Sonali crossed her arms. "I want to be the shopkeeper too." Vasudha looked at her caps. "Then it's a big shop. You sell vegetables, I sell sweets." Sonali nodded, then added, "And at lunch the shop closes." They both pretended to lock a gate.

qa.q: What did Vasudha use to set up her shop?
qa.a: She used leaves and bottle caps on a step.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when she crossed her arms?
qa.a: She was likely annoyed or left out, wanting to be the shopkeeper rather than only the buyer.

qa.q: How could a parent passing by support their game?
qa.a: They could stop to buy something from the shop, adding to the story without taking it over.

qa.q: What would change if Vasudha had refused to share the shop?
qa.a: Sonali might have walked off and the game would end, instead of growing with her idea about lunchtime.

grounding: Two girls in an Indian city negotiate roles and add to a shared pretend shop story.

passage:
"I'm the Amma. You be the Appa, Rajni."
"No, I'm the Amma too. Two Ammas."
"Two Ammas? Okay. Then who makes the food?"
"You make rice. I make chutney."
"And the baby is crying!" Urmila picked up the doll.
"She is hungry," said Rajni. "Give her milk."
"She's sleeping now. Shh."
"Now we go to the temple, and the baby comes too."
They tucked the doll into a dupatta sling and marched to the door.

qa.q: What food did Rajni say she would make?
qa.a: She said she would make chutney.

qa.q: Why does Rajni want to be an Amma too?
qa.a: She wants the important role in the game rather than a part she likes less, so she suggests having two Ammas.

qa.q: How did the girls keep the game going smoothly?
qa.a: They agreed quickly on two Ammas and split the cooking, then kept adding new parts to the story.

qa.q: How might a parent listening see this game?
qa.a: They might enjoy how the girls mix home life into play and settle their own disagreements without help.

grounding: Two girls negotiate roles and plot in a dialogue-driven game of house.

passage: In the colony park, Saurabh and Pranav both grabbed the plastic cricket bat. "Mine first!" Pranav tugged and Saurabh fell back on the grass. He started to cry. Pranav stood holding the bat, then walked over. "Sorry. I pulled too hard." Saurabh sniffed. "You bat for five balls, then me." "Okay." Pranav counted each ball aloud, then handed the bat over. By evening they were yelling "Out!" together.

qa.q: Where were Saurabh and Pranav playing?
qa.a: They were playing in the colony park.

qa.q: What might Pranav have felt when Saurabh fell and cried?
qa.a: He likely felt guilty or worried, which is why he stood still and then walked over to apologise.

qa.q: What was helpful about Saurabh's idea of five balls each?
qa.a: It gave a clear, fair rule for turns that both boys could follow and check by counting.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see Pranav after the apology?
qa.a: He may feel respected again and willing to keep playing because Pranav admitted his mistake.

grounding: Two boys resolve a fight over a bat with an apology and an agreed turn-taking rule.

passage:
"It's my car! Give it!"
"I had it first, Kishore!"
"Boys," Ammi called from the kitchen, "what can you do with one car?"
Kishore frowned. "Tanvir drives it to the garage, then I drive it back."
Tanvir thought. "Okay. But I get the garage part."
"Fine."
A minute later: "Kishore, sorry I pushed you."
"It's okay. Sorry I shouted."
"Your turn now. Vroom!"
"Vroom!"

qa.q: Who called out to the boys from the kitchen?
qa.a: Ammi called to them from the kitchen.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir say sorry a minute later?
qa.a: He seems to have felt bad about pushing Kishore once they had calmed down and found a way to share.

qa.q: What made Ammi's question a good way to help?
qa.a: She did not choose a winner; she asked what they could do, so the boys came up with their own plan.

qa.q: What would change if Ammi had simply taken the car away?
qa.a: The fight would stop, but the boys would miss the chance to work out turns and say sorry by themselves.

grounding: Two brothers work out turns with one toy car and apologise to each other.

passage: Note to parents, Friday. At the puzzle corner, Irawati snatched the last piece from a classmate and he burst into tears. I knelt by them and asked, "What happened?" Irawati looked at the floor. "I wanted to finish it." After a moment she said, "Sorry," and handed it back. They agreed he would place the last piece, and she would choose the next puzzle. They did two more together. 🙂 I praised how they sorted it. — Dilnaz Ma'am

qa.q: What did Irawati snatch from her classmate?
qa.a: She snatched the last puzzle piece.

qa.q: What does Irawati looking at the floor suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt embarrassed or guilty about snatching, even before she apologised.

qa.q: How did the teacher support the children without taking over?
qa.a: She knelt, asked what happened, and let them agree on who would place the piece and choose the next puzzle.

qa.q: How might the classmate feel after getting the piece back?
qa.a: He would probably feel his upset was noticed and fairly repaired, making him happy to keep playing with Irawati. 🤍

grounding: A teacher records a child apologising and agreeing on turns after a puzzle dispute.

passage: Guests were due any minute, and the tin of buttons had spilled across the floor. Dilnaz Ammi groaned. "No time, beta." But Nirmala was already crouching. "Reds here, whites here, blacks here." Then she stopped. "This red one is big, it goes with the big ones." She made a line of big buttons and a pile of tiny ones. When the doorbell rang, three neat heaps sat back in the tin.

qa.q: What had spilled across the floor?
qa.a: The tin of buttons had spilled.

qa.q: How was Dilnaz Ammi feeling when she saw the spill?
qa.a: She felt stressed and hurried, groaning and saying there was no time because guests were due.

qa.q: How could Dilnaz Ammi encourage Nirmala's sorting later?
qa.a: She could ask her to explain her groups, like why the big red button went with the big ones.

qa.q: What would change if there had been no rush?
qa.a: Nirmala might have had time to try more ways of grouping, maybe by shape, and talk about each choice.

grounding: A girl sorts spilled buttons by colour and then by size while guests are about to arrive.

passage: In their Kolkata flat, Bhupen Dadu dumped a basket of dry socks on the bed. "Help me pair these, Maria." Maria, five, made piles. "Big ones are Papa's. Medium are Dadu's. Tiny ones are mine!" Then she held up two blue socks of different sizes. "Same colour, but not same size," she said, and put them in different piles. Dadu raised his eyebrows. "Clever girl."

qa.q: How did Maria sort the socks at first?
qa.a: She made piles by size: big for Papa, medium for Dadu and tiny for herself.

qa.q: How did Dadu feel about Maria's sorting?
qa.a: He seemed impressed, raising his eyebrows and calling her a clever girl.

qa.q: What small step could Dadu add to stretch her thinking?
qa.a: He could ask her to sort the same socks by colour next and compare the two ways.

qa.q: How might Papa benefit from Maria's sorting?
qa.a: His big socks end up together in one pile, making it easier for him to find a pair. 👍

grounding: A girl sorts laundry by size and notices that colour and size are different traits.

passage:
"Nandini, triangles go in this box."
"And circles here. What about this one, Anirban?"
"That's half a circle. It's round on one side."
"But it's flat on this side. It's not a circle."
"Make a new box for half-circles?"
"Yes! And squares go with... wait, this is long."
"That's a rectangle. It has four sides but it's longer."
"Rectangles get their own box too."
They lined up four boxes on the floor.

qa.q: How many boxes did they line up on the floor?
qa.a: They lined up four boxes.

qa.q: Why did Nandini disagree that the half-circle was a circle?
qa.a: She noticed it was flat on one side and felt it did not really belong with the round shapes.

qa.q: What was good about how they solved the half-circle problem?
qa.a: Instead of forcing it into a box, they made a new group for half-circles, which fit its shape.

qa.q: What would change if they sorted by colour instead of shape?
qa.a: The half-circle and rectangle puzzles might disappear, but new questions about colour groups would come up.

grounding: Two children sort blocks by shape and create new groups for shapes that do not fit.

passage: During recess at the school playground, Gurleen picked up a flat leaf and a twig. "This is my plate, and this is my spoon." Kiran grabbed a bigger stick. "This is my microphone! Welcome to the cooking show!" Gurleen served pebbles as "parathas" on her leaf. Kiran pretended to taste. "Too spicy!" he gasped, fanning his mouth. When the bell rang, Gurleen carefully tucked her leaf-plate under a bench for tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Kiran use as a microphone?
qa.a: He used a bigger stick as a microphone.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen tuck her leaf-plate under the bench?
qa.a: She wanted to keep it for tomorrow, showing the leaf still mattered to her as a real plate in their game.

qa.q: How could a teacher encourage this kind of play?
qa.a: Leave some natural bits like leaves and sticks around and ask the children about their pretend show.

qa.q: How might Kiran see Gurleen's pebble parathas?
qa.a: He treats them as real food, playing along and making the story funnier for both of them.

grounding: Two children use leaves, twigs and pebbles to stand for plates, spoons, food and a microphone.

passage: My brother Irfan is four. Yesterday he held Abbu's slipper to his ear and talked into it. "Hello, Nani? Yes, I ate lunch." I laughed and picked up the slipper to put it back. He shouted, "You cut my call!" and stomped off. Later he used a folded chapati as a boat in his plate and his spoon as a sail. I said sorry about the phone. — Harsha

qa.q: What did Irfan use as a phone?
qa.a: He held Abbu's slipper to his ear and talked into it.

qa.q: Why did Irfan shout and stomp off?
qa.a: He felt angry and resentful that Harsha had ended his pretend call; to him the slipper really was a phone.

qa.q: What could Harsha do next time to respect Irfan's pretend play?
qa.a: She could ask first, like "Can I have the phone after your call?", before moving his toy.

qa.q: How might Harsha see the slipper differently from Irfan?
qa.a: To Harsha it was just a slipper out of place, while to Irfan it was an important phone connected to Nani.

grounding: A sister describes her little brother using a slipper as a phone and a chapati as a boat, and his anger when the pretence is broken.

passage:
Monday: Vinita pushed a steel spoon along the table. "Vroom, car!" Her father Darshan asked, "Where is it going?" "School," she said.
Friday: She dragged an empty carton into the hall. "This is a boat. Papa, you're the fish." She paddled with a ruler.
The next Sunday: A towel became her cape, a hairbrush her phone and a cushion a sleeping horse. "Shh, Papa, Horsey is sleeping." Darshan tiptoed past.

qa.q: What did Vinita use as a car on Monday?
qa.a: She used a steel spoon as a car.

qa.q: What does Vinita's "Shh, Papa, Horsey is sleeping" show about her thinking?
qa.a: It shows she treats the cushion as a real horse she cares for and wants Papa to respect her pretend world.

qa.q: How did Darshan support her pretend play?
qa.a: He asked where the car was going and tiptoed past the sleeping horse, joining in without taking over.

qa.q: What is it like for Darshan to be part of this game?
qa.a: He gets pulled into her stories as a fish and a quiet passer-by, which lets him share her imagination. 😊

grounding: Over days, a girl uses more objects to stand for others in pretend play.
